newsitem.title: FRANCE: France, Corsica brace for end to guerrilla truce.
newsitem.headline: France, Corsica brace for end to guerrilla truce.

text.p: A small bomb exploded in Corsica on Friday as the troubled Mediterranean island and mainland France awaited the formal end of a separatist guerrilla "truce" already shattered by dozens of bomb attacks.

The 10-month-old truce declared by the hardline Corsican National Liberation Front (FLNC)-Historic Wing is due to expire on Saturday. But it has largely become a myth as attacks resumed after secret talks with Paris collapsed during the summer.

A small bomb went off outside the post office in the island town of Folelli early on Friday, causing no injuries and little damage. It was the first blast since a bomb last weekend at city hall in Bordeaux, where Prime Minister Alain Juppe is mayor.
Witnesses said Juppe's security had been reinforced. Police sharpshooters watched from roofs on Friday as he opened new medical facilities in Bordeaux, and extra police were on duty.

Guards were strengthened around public buildings in Paris. Extra police were despatched to Marseille, Nice and Lyon whose mayor, ex-premier Raymond Barre, recently caused a stir by saying: "If Corsicans want independence, let them have it."

Reinforcements were also sent to boost Corsica's 1,700 policemen, paramilitary gendarmes and crack police squads. Security officials said they feared attacks against conspicuous symbols of the French state and were on alert while keeping a low profile.
No one claimed responsibility for the Folelli bomb.

Some 20 post offices, often the only symbol of the central government in rural Corsica, have been bombed in recent weeks by separatists who have been seeking to loosen ties with the mainland in a two-decade-old, low-key guerrilla campaign.
Police said last month they had arrested two young men who confessed to carrying out six such attacks recently. They are now in a Paris prison awaiting trial.
The FLNC-Historic Wing claimed responsibility for the bomb at Juppe's office. The second Corsican attack on the mainland in a month, it led Paris to announce a crackdown on separatists.

Corsica's police chief Gerard Bougrier said police had for some time been stepping up searches for weapons -- a big task on an island whose 250,000 people have a tradition of owning weapons, if only for hunting in the densely wooded mountains.
There were conflicting calls for war and peace as the end of the "truce" approached.
The separatist group Fronte Ribellu (Rebel Front), an ally of the FLNC-Historic Wing, has called on the islanders to rise up against French "aggressors", branded "the hereditary enemy".
It threatened to kill anyone who helped police in the crackdown Juppe has vowed against the separatists, who are split into rival groups waging a bloody war against each other.
More moderate nationalists called for dialogue and warned Paris that a brutal crackdown could revive support for the hardliners, who have become increasingly isolated.
In Paris, the pro-government daily Le Figaro said the French people's patience was growing thin over the continuing trouble on an island heavily subsidised by the mainland.
"Each islander gets an average 27,000 francs ($5,400) in subsidies (annually). A record. But it's never enough...Violence and greed are the two bases of Corsican terrorism," it said.
It said the government must be firm but avoid falling into the trap of escalating violence that separatists hope for.
"Otherwise, France will some day...inflict the worst punishment on Corsica: grant it independence," it said.
